Of course, I have always been a major advocate of Bosnia-Herzegovina when others were advocates of Yugoslavia. I also was a major advocate of the fact that the victims should not go through the conflict, and yet they went through it. Yesterday, I stated that I had a premonition that the war would break out, that I was against it and that I participated in the effort to stop it. This is what I'm personally very proud of. For these reasons, a country with such a sensitive fabric needs a more careful approach. Throughout the war, and the postwar period, it turned out that the internal territorial political structure of this unfortunate land has become a crucial, a key, problem. This is why I thought, and I still hold this belief, that this sort of a concept that I respect, because I'm an intellectual, will not give any fruit, and neither in the report nor now have I tried to conceal my views. But these are my views and my views alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Isn't it your view, sir, that the two cultures, the Muslim culture and the Croat culture are incompatible and they cannot exist on the same territory?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not my culture, nor is it my view. I have been discussing the territorial structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 803.02? 803.02? Sir, this purports to be from an interview that you gave on the 21st of December, 1995, the Croatian version is available to you there if you'd like to refer to it. For the Court room, I would direct in the English version to the second page of the English version, and to the paragraph -- on the second page there is Mr. Markotic begins talking and then there is the first paragraph and it there is the second paragraph. It says these words: "The federation of Croats and Muslims but not the territory on which they live together seems to be the embryo of destabilisation of the Croatian national being. Those two cultures are incompatible and they could hardly be joined by the common territory." Isn't that what you said, sir, in December, 1995?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, on the basis of what you have shown to me here, yes, but if I may add, science attributes to a newspapers as sources of secondary nature. A journalist who quoted me here could have quoted me in many other terms and ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you specifically, do you affirm these are your words or not? Was it your position as stated in December, 1995, that the Muslim culture and the Croat cultures were incompatible?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1995, I don't think I have put it in these words, but of course, anybody can write whatever they want here because this is not what I believe and I hope that through everything I said so far, I was able Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. convince this Trial Chamber of the contrary, but of course people have the right to write whatever they want and in whichever manner they feel. But of course, I was not the reviewer of this text. But what sort of compatibility or incompatibility is being referred to here, of course, is a matter that can be debated for days, for months and for years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can have the usher's assistance, please in showing the witness 851.2? Is it not in your bundle?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It seems to me that it's not in the bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If it isn't, sir, my apology. It was an error. Could you please put that on the ELMO? Mr. Usher, there is apparently some additional copies. I'm told, Mr. President, that the Defence and the booths have been provided copies, I hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence hasn't got a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Then please, we will get extra copies, if it can be placed on the ELMO, please, Mr. Usher?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I insist on having a copy in my hands. I can not follow the text through an ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes it's a legitimate request. I think Judge Diarra will let you have hers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you Judge Diarra.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, again I only have this at the moment in English, but there is only one passage I'd like to direct your attention to. Sir, this appears to be another interview with you on the 8th of March, 1999, and were you not asked about the question of the situation of the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina -- excuse me, Mr. President, I see counsel on his feet so I won't finish my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I apologise to the learned friend. These again are new documents. We do not know their sources, where this was written, where this was published, where the interview took place, foundations must first be laid before the question is being put to the witness. This is not the way to work. Whichever paper drops from heaven into this courtroom should then be considered as an exhibit. Who participated in the interview? Who was the interviewer? When it took place and so on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yesterday we were provided with a list, and this list is listed this document. Unfortunately we don't have the contents in that bundle. This says Radio Bosnia-Herzegovina programme featuring the witness. Then in this document, it seems to me that it is the BBC summary of the broadcasts. That's the question I want to ask the Prosecutor to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let us hear the Prosecutor first.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Chamber is at this point in these proceedings seen a number of these documents. The BBC as the Chamber may know better than me, the BBC provides a service by which it monitors and follows broadcasts around the world and provides summaries or publications concerning those broadcasts. This particular issue, if you will, was put out on the 10th of March, 1999. The source was a radio interview, radio broadcast from Radio Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo, in the Serbo-Croatian language at 2.00 Greenwich Mean Time on the 8th of March, 1999 and it purports to be an interview with the Witness, and if he doesn't recall these words or denies that they are his words, then he can certainly do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yes, yes. Radio Bosnia-Herzegovina does not exist. I will prove it to you by way of hundreds and thousands of evidence, pieces of evidence. There is no such radio station that would be called Radio Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Could we all calm down for a moment and let's do this thing properly. Mr. Scott isn't allowed to give evidence any more than the defence is allowed to give evidence. But Mr. Scott what you should have done in my view and in my humble opinion is that you first of all should have asked this witness does he have any recollection of an interview on such and such a date, with such and such a person, and lay the foundation properly that way. It isn't right to, in my opinion, to present a document and then to purport to give evidence as to its source. This witness must first be given an opportunity to say, "Never in my life have I ever had an interview with anybody from the BBC or on Radio Bosnia-Herzegovina or I have frequently given interviews and I recall it." That's the time-honoured way to introduce a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Judge Clark, I appreciate your guidance on that. I don't disagree with you, of course. The only reason I gave the answers that I gave was in response to the direction of the President based on the issue raised by council. Had that not happened I would simply have put it in front of the witness and asked about the conversation without having gone into all that. But I appreciate your guidance. I'll simply ask him that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall giving an interview on a radio station in Bosnia-Herzegovina sometime in 1999, around the 8th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since August, 1992, I never gave any interview to Radio Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So you simply deny that this interview took place at all? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know at all what interview you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, this purports to be -- and again I don't want to give evidence either, as Judge Clark says, this purports to be a record of an interview you gave and all I can ask you, as the Chamber has guided me, is, is it just simply your position that no such interview ever took place in which you talked about the need for a separate Croat entity?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not to Radio Bosnia-Herzegovina, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, can I help you this way? If one reads the document, it actually describes who was there at a round table discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So perhaps if you put to this witness, does he remember giving a radio interview at which the following people were present and the interview took place in Sarajevo around the 8th of March, 1999, he may object to the name of the station, as Mr. Krsnik clearly does.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me make certain, simply going from working from this document, and I'd certainly do not profess to have any information different than what's -- I can simply read. Sir, do you recall being involved in a conference in Sarajevo around March, 1999, where a number of people were present, including the Croat member, the then Croat member of the Bosnian Presidency, Ante Jelavic, other people were the mayor of Mostar at that time, Ivan Prskalo, other people, another person was Jusuf Muslimovic, at which there were discussions apparently of various issues concerning Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Dayton agreement at that time? Do you remember attending such a gathering in Sarajevo in approximately March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember great many things that have to do with Sarajevo because I've been living in Sarajevo for 30 years but this is simply not true. In Sarajevo, I never ever, after the year 1992, said in an interview, I had an opportunity to give an interview, I've been invited to give them, but no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you, apart from this document, sir, in 1999, was it your position, you told us a few moments ago that you were candid about your views, was it your position that without a Croat entity, a Croat identity or the survival of Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina is not possible? Was that your view in 1999?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the way you have put it, but in essence, yes, and this is true even today, because a nation who lost half its members in the course of the war, whose birth rates have been dropping, who has been emigrating over 50 years, well, you can statistically calculate that should this trend continue, will have disappeared sooner or later. And this is the whole truth. How people can understand it, of course, is a matter of manipulating the facts and statements. And of course, I am a familiar person in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I can't say that people haven't been manipulating with my statements, views, et cetera. It's very easy to claim that and Anto Markotic said something in connection with that. Yesterday, in my testimony, I said that I am Ante F. Markotic. And this is how I have been signing all my publications and all my books, because there are other persons by the name of Ante Markovic -- Markotic, sorry, with the same academic titles. I do not want to harm any one of them. However, I also do not want to be held responsible for their omissions. That is the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, just to be clear, then, and this is I think my final question to you: You said just a moment ago, and I'm looking at line 23 of page 51 of the transcript, "in essence, yes, this is true even today." That's your position, correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What are you asking me about?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions. However, I would feel the need to tell the Chamber -- and I apologise for not having a rule. I was off by one. I'm afraid when I referred the Chamber to H, the Rule 90(H) sub-Roman numeral ii, I should have been referring the Chamber at least in part to H (i), which simply provides that cross-examination shall be limited to the subject matter of evidence-in-chief and matters affecting the credibility of the witness and where the witness is able to give evidence relevant to the case of the cross-examining party to the subject matter of the case. I'm not arguing with the Court's ruling but I couldn't find that before and I'm just simply pointing it out. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Re-examination, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I'm glad that the Prosecutor has read this H (i) And I wish he had been sticking to that rule while he was cross-examining my 35 witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, I know that you have been here for two days and you're finding it difficult.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you for your understanding. I'm trying to understand your profession, I'm trying to understand your colourful style, and now I understand how important it is when you are interpreting boring figures to the lay persons, how important it is to be interesting and colourful. I'm going to give you this map number P947, and I'm going to ask you one question. If this is scientifically valuable, if the map has not been made according to the rules of demographic profession, in order to provide this Chamber with an accurate answer, I'm going to ask my learned friend Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to give us the name of the person who has authored this map, not just the Prosecution, but the name, the first and the last name, of the author of the map. I assume that this may be Mrs. Ewa Tabeau, that is my assumption but I would like confirmation of that from my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I believe that would be true, Mr. President, either her or people working directly with her. Off the top of my head, I couldn't be more specific than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I'm sorry, of this map, and I know a lot about Mrs. Ewa Tabeau. My question to you is as follows and I'm asking you for a very concise answer, please focus on the essence and then give us the explanation. If such a map does not follow the rules of science, the rules of the United Nations, can such a map be valid? Does it have any value?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are putting me a very professional question, and I'll try to be as brief as possible. My maps lack a lot. This map lacks a lot. But I have to ask all of you not to read the fate of a state or of a people from simplified, colourful maps. They will not tell you anything about the destiny, about the history, culture and relationships amongst peoples. They are just a methodological simplified procedure which reveals the complexity of the structure of any one society. They cannot suffice, they are not enough, what I usually say to my students is this: What you cannot explain well enough, try to represent it graphically, in simplified ways. Another rule: What you draw, you don't have to explain, and what is clear does not have to be drawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Professor, can you give me a specific answer, if possible? It says on the map, 1997, as the year of its publication. If such a map did not respect the rules of the profession in 1997, would this map have any value?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The value of this map would be relative but that is the same thing that applies to my map dating from 1996, because it was based on non-official data, which have not been checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Professor, these maps serve to determine the destiny of people in this Court. Can you please establish a connection between that map and the map that I'm going to ask the usher to give to you? This is P1899. What is the connection between these two maps? And before that, have you ever seen the demographic map of the so-called banovina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: He answered that quite clearly, he's never seen a map of the banovina. Also, you seem to be almost cross-examining your witness, Mr. Krsnik. He said to us that the map from the OTP and his maps are both illustrative, they are not intended to be used as anything else except to show people who are less clever than he is, his point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour Judge Clark. I'm using the style of cross-examination. I thought maybe this would guide professor better. I would help him. I would help him to give me concise answers. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, I think you should know your expert. Like a lot of professors, he's not easily influenced.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will be very happy if the professor gives me an opportunity to become his acquaintance, if not his friend, because I've learned a lot from him. What I'm trying to say, Your Honour, is there is a huge difference between the map from 1996 and 1997. And this 1997 map is used to determine the destiny of some people in this court, and still there is a huge drastic difference between these two maps. This is what I'm trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, please, look at the second map and tell us whether there is any connection, any link, between the map that I have just given to you and the map that you had before?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not want to say anything when I saw the resemblance between this map and my map. What I'm trying to say is that none of them can serve to prove anything for the other, no matter what from what direction you approach it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: No. This is not what I meant. Is there any connection between the map of the so-called banovina and the so-called demographic map?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can make anything with Lego bricks. What I'm saying is that maps of this kind are not a stable source.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please check some transcripts from some other cases? Because now the counsels have started joining forces. Our opponent is very strong, has databases, has computers, so I'm going to offer you one transcript to illustrate how the Prosecution in some other cases claims and asserts very different things and I'm going to show you how they conflict each other from one case to another. I've just received an expert's letter from another case, and I believe that it will be very important that you read it in this case as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, again, let me explain. I don't like to interrupt counsel and I try not to do that but again we get to these situation where we are having these discussions in front of the witness and there is no choice. Once the words are said, it's too late. So counsel, subject to the Chamber's direction, counsel can certainly submitted whatever he wants to you, subject again to your views but we don't need to have this discussion in front of the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I don't think it is wrong for Mr. Krsnik to raise this issue after the witness has left this courtroom. Do you have any other questions, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I feel the need to apologise. I just wanted to say that I believe that I have the same rights as the -- my learned friend. Never has the Prosecution witness left this courtroom when we had similar discussions before, but I do apologise if I have made a mistake or if I have been rude. I have another question, Your Honour. We are approaching the break time, and if this courtroom will allow me, I will put that question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to ask you to have the break first, to allow me to concentrate on that question and then to put the question to the witness after the break, if I may suggest that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if you prefer, it seems to me that you ask very complicated questions. Then we will break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I just want to ask a couple of questions, professor Markotic so that my question may then subsequently become the subject matter of the other questions at the break. And the President has given me leave, and if you don't mind, Mr. Scott, and Mr. Krsnik, this document which has caused us all to become quite cross, indicates, professor Markotic that was reviewed by professor doctor Ante Markotic. Before we go into any discussion which will happen later, can I just establish that that is you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Well, this is the question which has since the document has been produced has caused me to be very curious. Why would a scientist of your standing, professor Markotic, an expert in demography, review a paper on military history? I'm curious about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Luckily enough today we can communicate by e-mail so you don't have to see the person whose text you're asked to review. Where I come from, things are different. I graduated from a university but in my village, there is no electricity. People lived like they do. And an old -- and a grammar school teacher asks somebody to be his reviewer if they hold him in high esteem and another part of the story could be educational. Many texts, unlike previously, have been written about this war and published about this war. There are no standards. There is no protection of copyright. There is no possibility to correct the mistakes or correct the opinions for which at one point, I thought that it was my interview given in Sarajevo in 1999. Similar things after the end of the war, and especially during the war, were ample, and many. It is possible to answer your question in different ways. Now, I believe I share your views. When I reviewed this book, I thought differently. Now I'm closer to your views. Obviously at that time I thought that somebody who collected documents that these documents should be kept for posterity. Any kinds of documents. And you may well know that these books contain a lot of material which lend themselves to further research and today, research has not been completed. Even for the Second World War. The Second World War is still being researched and investigated. And these documents are covering the events that took place in the past war, in the war in Bosnia. The motive that I had at the time was, "let's preserve the documents and it is the responsibility of the author for the documents that he has placed in that book." For example, the victims of the war, you have certainly heard here that some people testified although they were "rest in peace" before that, a long time before that, so that would be my reason for signing the review, together with the other reviewer of this book. I spoke sincerely and in the way I feel it. Maybe I have used too many words for the brief -- for the short question that you have asked me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Could we say, then, professor Markotic, that you reviewed the documents and the -- obviously the papers before they were published, to lend your name to something that you approved of, which was the preservation of facts arising out of a period of turmoil?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: analyse either the author or his text. He himself analysed the text. Maybe I or somebody else would have done something else with the same documents, but this is the author's choice to do whatever he wants to do with the documents, to present them in any way he wants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that gives both parties food for thought over the break, and they may wish to ask further questions. Mr. Krsnik clearly doesn't. But I'm very much assisted by your answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll resume at ten minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I did not see Mr. Scott in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, he's somewhere around. He's coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So we'll wait for him for a few minutes, just to be fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you for your cooperation. Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Professor, I don't want to keep you much longer. I just want to ask you two questions, if possibly clever questions, if I know how to do that. The first question -- let's say that Dayton borders, from 1995, Bosnia and Herzegovina, prior to the Dayton and after the Dayton, what kind of a scientific research should be done with regard to the fact that you said that there was -- there hasn't been any census since 1991? What kind of a scientific research should be carried out in order for such a scientific research to be credible in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in any of its municipalities, the issue of that scientific research would be were there any persecutions, ethnic persecutions in any municipality in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Which scientific research would answer that question with a high degree of credibility?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once the census is carried out, it will not provide you with an answer to the question that would have a high degree of credibility for each and every case. And what I'm saying is that each and every case is similar to any other case, and also similar to the persecution of a whole. Given the fact that we do not have that, we use the usual methods and those methods are scientific studies or expertise. Obviously, one person is always limited. Two are less limited. If there is five scientists, their findings will be better. A scientific research, like a case study, would provide a more -- most credible picture. But even then, without certain documents, without certain scientific research on a certain sample, I cannot explain here what a sample is, what a case study is, so such a research would provide you with a better assessment, given the fact that you do not have everything that is necessary for such an assessment to be made. So without specific studies, that would cover every house, every apartment, there will always be ample room for asking yourself whether your data are accurate and how accurate they are. If this answers your question in principle, I would end with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. This was just an introduction to my next question. Let's take the example of Mostar, where you carried your research. Did you use this methodology, in addition to the written sources? Did you have associates? Did you go from one house to another? How scientific is your analysis of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I answered that question yesterday. Today I have repeated some things. I was on my own. I used with whatever was available at the time. And that is what I quoted in my study. I admitted, before this Honourable Chamber, that this method leaves a lot to be desired, and I said that I did what I did on the basis of what I quoted, and I also claimed that what I had established may be denied, may be questionable, and may be improved by some other findings. For as long as these other new findings are not available, I will believe that I am the most credible, subject to verification. I said that there are different cases and that these cases cannot just be regarded statistically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, professor. And my last question: I have in front of me a document that the Prosecutor has used for his cross-examination. The number is P100.01. What I'm going to ask you is whether on the 17th of August, in 1991, did you sign a pro memoria for the salvation of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo? And who else was there as the signatory to this document?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: 17 August, 1991.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that I know of that aide-memoire, but if you are asking for an explicit answer, then I can say that I did not sign that aide-memoire, and I can add to that this document, I have subsequently learned, so that this document was allegedly signed by some dozen intellectuals who, as far as I can remember, were all Croats. At the time on that day, I was in Herzegovina, in Neum. I remember very well. But I do not remember the date. I was with my wife, and I was talking to one of her authors, Milan Stojic, who read several paragraphs to me and explained the rest, and if you will allow me to finish, I can say that today I would sign that part that was read to me. But then later on, when I read the integral text, I saw one part that says, more or less as follows: In case of a conflict, of a war, between Croatia and Serbia, i.e. between Serbia and Croatia, Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina must remain neutral. And for that reason, I wouldn't sign this document. And the rest you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: By the way --

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You should ask its other signatories whether they would sign this document. You should ask its authors whether they would draft it in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Professor, I respect your answer, but I have to tell you that we lawyers do not use metaphors and poetic language in either indictments or in courtrooms. Here it says for a fact that you signed this document.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not. I've signed a hundred others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But look at the second page.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am one of those people who have learned from newspapers that they had signed this document. I have just explained that I didn't and why I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: This is all I wanted to ask you. We have dealt here with all sorts of documents, with all sorts of signatures. And with all sorts of people. Thank you very much. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions from the Judges? Yes, Judge Diarra, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you, Your Honour. Professor, I apologise for going beyond the scope of demography, of demographic science. Given the information that you have presented to us about the relationship between the underdeveloped economy and the tensions between the three peoples, not for a single moment did I hear you mentioning the term "citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina." You have been referring to the three constituent peoples in this state. Following your logic, and according to your opinion, every form of government must undergo the judgement of all the three constituent peoples, or are you maybe implying that some day it may be resolved in the way that all the citizens, all the inhabitants, of Bosnia-Herzegovina may decide that? I accord to lot of importance to your answers and I would be very interested in hearing what you think on that.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm very glad that I have heard somebody speaking French. This is my second language. I trust your trust. Very many times I have mentioned the things that you have quoted. It is not my personal opinion, it is not my personal view, when I say how a state should be organised. It is not up to me to believe or not believe in what you have said. But yesterday and today, I have tried to concentrate in as much as I can do it as a demographer and a native of that area, as a professor and as an intellectual, on something that I believe I should spread as my mission. I said that it is the most intimate right of any individual to have its attitude towards himself, his origin, his culture, his people, his religion. Yesterday, I said, and I repeat it today, that you cannot expect from any one people to skip centuries in just one generation. You cannot expect somebody who believed in God only yesterday to say today that there is no God. Illiterate people can do little. Semi-literate people can do something. Literate people can do a lot. However, the problem does not lie in the way I think -- see things. When a family is poor, and when that same family has a lot of children, they will all get little. It will be the mother who will cut the bread and will give to each child as much as she can. In any one society, in any village, town, municipality, things cannot be the same as they are in a family. When you have little, and when you give a lot to ones and little to others, then problems arise. And then we get -- arrival at a situation in which illiterate, literate and very literate people behave differently. The large masses, masses of the population, felt the injustice. You're signalling me to finish. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of Judges' questions? Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, as I've done before I'm going to be perfectly transparent with the Chamber and will only go forward based on the Chamber's guidance. Before the break, Judge Clark indicated, asked some questions about the witness's involvement with this publication by Mr. Rotim. If that's considered within the scope of Judge's questions, then I would have -- then I do have questions about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have to object. Back on page 44, when this issue arose, you made a ruling at that point in time, and it started at line 2 on page 44, and it ended at line 8. And you said "at this moment, this witness is not going to testify on that issue. It is so decided." Then, on page 59, after you had denied Mr. Scott, my learned colleague, and properly so because this expert is on demographics, and I will never object when a Judge asks a question while they are asking a question, but it seems to it me that on page 59, Her Honour Judge Clark asked the same questions that you denied Mr. Scott to ask concerning that document. That's the way I read the transcript, Your Honour. That's the way I see it. I believe in this Tribunal that the Prosecutor has a job, the Defence counsel has a job, and Your Honours have a job. You're the triers of fact, you're the triers of law. And I don't believe that my client can get a fair trial when the Judges start doing the Prosecutor's job. And it just appears that that has been happening sometimes, and I believe this is a good example, because, Your Honour, Mr. President, page 44, you told the Prosecutor that this witness is not a proper witness to ask about this document because he's an expert on demographics. He was stopped from that line of questioning but it came back up on page 59. I want it make a record on it and that's all I'm doing. Thank you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Meek, I think that you do me an injustice in your criticism. I did not ask this witness anything whatever about the content of the document. I asked him why would a demographer and a scientist review a paper on military history. And at no stage was he asked about the content. I asked him first of all, did he actually edit it? Because he said that he signed his name differently. And secondly, if he did, if he said, "well, I didn't edit it," there is no point asking the question. What I wanted to know is why would a demographer, a person who is presented here as an expert in demography, edit what is clearly a book on military history. Nobody asked him about the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour. I thank you very much and I appreciate what you say, but I'm looking at page 59 and specifically I'm looking at your comment starting on line 14 where you asked the witness, "Obviously the papers before they were published, to lend your name to something that you approved of," and here is where I think it's important, "Which was the preservation of facts arising out of the period of turmoil." When you asked that question about facts, preserving facts, to me that means the facts that were contained in that document. Whatever they might be. That's my concern, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: If you look at the response, Mr. Meek, that the witness made to my question, it was that this man was somebody who was interested in preserving documents and facts. And he thought that that was important. And all I was doing was trying to summarise and to understand why he endorsed. Somebody of his standing gave his name to this person, in order that he would endorse what he was doing. That is preserving facts for posterity. Which is what the response that he gave. I think is what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: But my point is, Your Honour, and perhaps I've misread or misconstrued this but with the question of preserving the facts that indicates to me that Your Honour feels the facts or whatever facts may be that document are true. We don't know who the author is. The author is not here. The author hasn't been brought. This is a demographer. He's not a military expert. The providing Judge Liu said he couldn't go into this these questions and now Mr. Scott wants to go back into this question about this document and we object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, no, no. Well, we allowed Mr. Scott to ask a question within the scope of the questions raised by the Judges, which does not mean that we allowed Mr. Scott to go into the content of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I guess we will wait and see what the questions are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in light of what's just been said, I presume you've heard all this, I'm not asking -- the question I'm about to ask you -- I'm not asking you about anything in the content, in the text of the book, if the main portion of the book or either book as it there were two volumes, but sir, not only does your name appear, is it correct, in the front binder of the book as the reader or reviewer, but in fact, in volume 1, sir, you and your co-reviewer, Mr. Maric, wrote a two and a half page what we might call forward to the book, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I signed Maric's two pages. I did not write them myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, that's interesting in other ways, sir, because we have had a lot of testimony in this case about signing documents. So in other words, your testimony here is, under oath, that you didn't write the forward on pages 17, 18 and 19 of the book, but you simply signed your name to something that Mr. Maric wrote? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Could we have 17, 18 and 19? I don't believe they have been given to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll be more than happy to. If I can have the usher's assistance, please. If I could have the usher's assistance, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, a misunderstanding here. The gentleman has just said that he did not sign these two pages, and I am not -- sorry, he did not write. He did not author these two pages. So I couldn't care less what it says in the text. What matters here to Mr. Scott is for you to get the document and read it. This is the game that Mr. Scott has been playing a lot of times. That's why we get just excerpts from documents in the binders and the rest you will get later on. That's the game that my learned friend is -- has been playing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Here they are. We'll give him the whole book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I think the Prosecutor distributed those documents at the request of Mr. Meek. Since we are talking about this document, I think better that we have it for reference. Yes, Mr. Scott. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, as I said at the very beginning I've been as transparent about it as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, please -- please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an insult for my intellectual integrity and my knowledge that I have acquired over the past 20 years all over the world. I'm not a child. Maybe the transcript is wrong. Mr. Prosecutor is trying to get this, to get to you. He wants you to read it. He is not interested in the witness's answer. There is no other way for this document to reach you. This is the only thing that the Prosecution is interested in. This is inadmissible because we already said that this witness cannot talk about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I understand what you're saying. The document we are provided in Croatian, so we are not able to read it. At least at this moment. What we are interested in is only the signature on the last page of this document. If this Trial Chamber considers that it's out of the scope of the testimony of this witness, we will certainly return this document to the Prosecution without reading it. Yes, Mr. Scott. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if the document requested by counsel has been provided to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I know this is going to provoke further outcry by counsel but I don't know of any way to handle a document in the courtroom without it being marked for the record, especially given the disputes that have been raised now, so I'm going to ask that document which was just handed out a few moment ago to be marked, please, at 927/4. There will be no dispute in the record in the future of what we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you have that document, I assume that you do, so I'm now going to refer to it for the record purposes as 927/4. On page 19, sir, your name appears along with Mr. Maric's name; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I want to be very clear that I -- if we understand your testimony a few minutes ago, are you saying that you did not write any of the text above your name, starting on page 17 of the book -- excuse me, yes, page 17, page 18 and the top half of page 19 that appears over your name? Is it your testimony that you did not take any part, play any role, in preparing that text or any part thereof?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct. However, I was read out this text in -- before proofreadings were carried out, when it was printed by a printing machine, and not in the manner in which it has been put in front of me now, not in the manner in which the book was eventually printed. I must, however, admit that I did not follow the destiny of these two pages, which I did not author, but having been read these two pages to me by Mr. Maric, I signed them. Whether this is the same or a different text, I really couldn't be the judge of that, but the possibility is there that the other names, that the names were left but the text had been changed. Something else: In both versions, in the first and in the second volume, I was the second mentioned in the text. It is namely customary that for a professional review or the reading of somebody else's manuscript, be done by the first professional reviewer. I was not the first professional reviewer, but in both volumes, as I can see it now, I was put as the first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To your earlier question --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the earlier question of the Honourable Chamber, I answered in the following manner. I did what I did, but I'd like to add now, on the basis of what I can see here, that the book did not undergo the usual procedure which any public publication should go through. For example, I see no numbers concerning the degree -- decrees passed by the Ministry of Culture. I don't see the ISBN number, and so on. So this was my additional view and statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you said a moment ago and I'll read it back to you in the transcript if you wish me to, that it was the person listed first who had the principal reviewer's role and I'd like you to be shown, please, Exhibit 8927/2, the one previously marked, 927/2 was the excerpt before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I put a question to you, Your Honours? Please instruct me. Do we really have to lose so much time on something for which this witness hadn't been invited here in the first place so that the Prosecutor will push through a text that he wants you to read?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, this issue has been brought up in the cross-examination. Then Judge Clark asked a question about it. I believe it will be fair to both parties to let the Prosecution continue his question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Rule 20(H)(i) had just been read out and one of the basic principles is that I never was allowed to put this question in my direct examination. If we are talking in the first place about rules and procedures, in direct examination, this was not the subject of any question. This was then done outside the direct examination. And this is Rule 90(H)(i). One cannot go beyond the scope of the direct examination in cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, we believe that those questions raised in the cross-examination by the Prosecutor have something to do with the credibility of this witness. Because this witness came here as an expert witness, and in the meantime, he also participated in other functions, other works. Yes, you may proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you have Exhibit 927/2 in front of you again, in the front of that book, and if you like you can look at both volumes of the original, you were listed as the first reviewer and by your testimony, the person with the principal responsibility for reviewing the material, correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said the opposite, but it turned out the way it is printed in the book. However, I see no official decree approving the publishing of this book, which would also give a special significance to my review. With your permission, I'd like to add the following: That this happened in 1994. However, here, I can see the years 1997 and 1998 printed. In other words, a lot of these matters are disputable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, did you say that in these materials now, these forwards and parts, beginnings of the book, did you say, well a lot of this material is really not reliable but I'll put my signature, I'll put my name on it any way? Can you tell us please somewhere in that forward that I handed you where you said that?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my recollection, I said that this was written in 1994. It was read out to me while I was sitting at a table. I cannot recall it, however, and I don't know either what is written down here now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, in addition to what we have just been handed out a moment ago as 927/4, did you not also personally write, in fact over -- under your name also an introduction to the first volume? And I will show you what I'll ask to be marked as 927/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, while this is being handed out, I am going for the record to make another objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: 30 pages ago, on page 44, you ruled that the Prosecutor, that this was not the proper witness for this Prosecutor to ask questions about. He's a demographer, he's an expert and because on page 59, Her Honour Judge Clark asked two questions about this, now we are Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. going back into more detail about an issue that you have already ruled on 30 pages ago. And we strongly object to this. This expert witness is on demography and now Mr. Scott is trying to turn him into something else and it's just improper and it does not go to credibility whatsoever. That's a guise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I couldn't disagree more. Let me again -- I don't know how any more transparent I could be. Am I interested in this the content of this book yes, I am absolutely. Whether this is the appropriate witness or not separate matter. But it does go to his credibility. He's talked about his role in this book and he's gone back -- I don't want to argue this in front of the witness. I think it's directly relevant to the credibility. It also is exactly the kind of situation that I referred the Chamber to it earlier on (H)(i) and where the witness is able, he's come to The Hague, where the witness is able to give evidence relevant to the case for the cross-examining party, that is here the Prosecution, relevant to the subjects matter of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, we are not going to debate legal issues before the witness. If you ever questions, please ask your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We have made that ruling that those questions are related to the credibility of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If the witness can be shown Exhibit 927/3? Which is a new -- that's the one I just handed out, Your Honour. Sir, this is the further introduction or beginning of the second volume of the book starting at page 14 and going over to page 16, another two and a half pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We've just been told by the Prosecutor that -- well, in the book it says 1997, 1998. Could, please, we be told where this text comes from? Which book, which year, which volume? Because the Prosecutor was referring to 1994 before. And the witness was talking about 1994 and repeated it time and again. We have just been given a few pages of a text and we would very much appreciate it if we knew where this text comes from. An and then the witness might be able to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: This is also the question we want to ask. Mr. Scott, would you please furnish us with more information about this piece of document?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. 927/4, which was handed out a few moments ago, comes from volume 1 of the two volume set. I'm holding up volume 1 now. It was published in Siroki Brijeg in 1997. It was -- Mr. Markotic is listed as the first reviewer. And the usual -- I suppose the usual kind of publication information that I'm familiar with is included. There is a glossary in the back, there is terms, there is credits for other people's contributions. So that's the book that I'm referring to. For Exhibit 927/3, is material from the second volume of the book published in Siroki Brijeg in 1998, again listing Mr. Markotic as the first reviewer, and in that volume, 927.-- Exhibit 927.3, starting at page 14, Mr. Markotic appears under his name, to write a 2 and a half page whatever, introduction, review, forward, to the book. And that's the source of the material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in connection with volume 2, because you said earlier that you wrote -- that the introduction or forward in volume 1, you couldn't remember --

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is not what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, since I didn't finish my question, perhaps you'd let me finish it. You said, sir, that you did not write that document but some parts of it were read to you and you gave your name to it, correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in the second -- and in volume 2, in a similar fashion, you wrote a two and a half page or did you write it? That's my question. Did you write and did you give your name once again to two and a half pages of material about volume 2?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But that was done much earlier, on a different piece of paper, and then I did not follow the fate of this paper afterwards. Because obviously, what is in front of me, comparing -- comparing it to what I was -- I had in front of me which was a manuscript is quite a different story. It would have been fair and honest from the author to inform me what would be the destiny of the manuscript later on but let us not forget this was during the war. I was a refugee, I didn't have a home. And I already told the Honourable Chamber what were the circumstances, and I still claim that there is no official version of this book. The author and the first reviewer, which is in the first place for reasons explained before, may have been done by the other reviewer, by the author of the text, they could have done whatever they preferred. I didn't have an insight into the later destiny of this text. What was read to me is, as far as I can recall, was different from what you asked me, whether I approved in one of your questions. So I would humbly ask you to be allowed to defend my own credibility, if possible, as an expert witness in front of this Honourable Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in the book, and I'll refer back to 927/2, since that's the one that has at least some translation of, it's from the second volume, 927/2, again, just to be clear, there is other persons below you and Mr. Maric's name, which are given the roles of language editing and proofreading. There are three individuals given the name excuse me given the role of computer layout. So, sir, can we understand from that that your role had something more to do than computer layout and language editing and proofreading? Your role was much more substantial than that, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any event, you don't have to ask me about that. But the publishing house is not mentioned, which was supposed to have received a decree from somebody. This, as far as I can see, is the author's Karlo Rotim's personal publication. The difference in terms of the years of publication is something that I'm trying to point out. What I had been read out was in 1994. These books have the years 1997, 1998. What I signed is something that was printed by a printing machine. What happened Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to that text, as I said before, I could not follow. I can't recall it. And I wasn't even interested in it. Because I believe that the reviewer is not responsible for the contents of the text that he did not contribute to. And I am not responsible for the text that you have given to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you said yourself that in 1994, the war was still going on. Is it not reasonable to conclude or infer that that material may not have been -- until 1997?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, didn't we get 101st answer to one and the same question? Do we really need to proceed? I numbered it. For 20 times, one and the same question was put, and one and the same answer was given. I think everything is clear. And what I am now happy to learn is that this book never was publicly published. I should like to thank the learned friend for raising this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I believe you're giving the testimony yourself again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You're giving a hint to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, Your Honour. The witness answered it for 20 times, that this book never was published officially. This is what the witness answered for 20 times, that this is a personal circulation, a personal publication, of the author, for 20 times he answered it, and I don't know what is put in the transcript but that is what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We are not discussing this issue at this moment. Mr. Scott, we hope you could wind up your re-examination as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm finished, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I apologise. Just one clear and loud question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Was this book ever published and made available to the public in a library or in a book shop?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall this procedure having been respected, with regard to this book, but as far as I can see it, I think that this is a Samizdat, a self publication by the author and the reviewer's text is usually not taken care of by the author. It is usually submitted to the publishing house and the publishing house obviously decides how to proceed. This is of course, a free market project. People can publish their own private publications. But they differ from the official publications. You can ask me about these details concerning my book, whenever the author has acted the way this author seems to have acted, is indeed not serious. And it is not fair for him to bring me into this position. I don't recall any such thing having been done to any of my books, but of course, this is not my book. This is some other author's book and I couldn't follow everything that went on. And of course, I couldn't check and double check whether the text of my review, which I had written, had also been published. Of course, this is my personal error, my personal omission, but I insist that I am not -- I was not the first reviewer, although I was put on first place in this book. I did not write it, and these are matters of fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much, professor. Frankly speaking, I myself benefit a lot from your expert testimony, since I came from a country with the largest population in the world. The usher will show you out of the room, and we all wish you a pleasant journey back home. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Meek? Do you have any documents to tender into the evidence at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I put it in writing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'll have it filed either tomorrow or Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may be allowed, I'll do the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Well, there are three matters I want to say about the proceedings. The first one is that as Defence counsel for Naletilic told us, the next expert witness will be the common witness for both parties, so we will arrange the hearing for the next witness during the course of Mr. Martinovic's case. Is that agreeable, Mr. Par? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We agree, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And on the 15th of July, we will start Mr. Martinovic's case. And we will start at 3.30 in the afternoon because this courtroom will be used by other proceedings. The last matter is Mr. Par, did your Defence team prepared to deliver an opening statement at the start of your case?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. On the first day of our opening statements, we will be able to present our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your information. The opening statement is just a summary of your case, not the process of presenting the evidence. So I hope you could do it in a very concise way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we plan to finish the opening statements on the very same day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One day is all we'll need for the opening statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So this Chamber will rise until 15th of July. Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, one thing and we will see you on the 15th of July. It's my understanding that we are in the afternoon session in Courtroom I, the rest of July. Is that correct? And in September?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, 3.30, I think is afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I understand, but I understand that the schedule in September because we are sharing Courtroom I and we have to go every afternoon or have night court and I just ask Your Honour to maybe talk to somebody in the Presidency, I do not believe Judge May and his Trial Chamber is any more important in this Trial Chamber and why should he get the morning sessions every morning? We should split it one week and one week. That's my request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Certainly, I will convey your views to the President of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Up to now I haven't received the Court schedule for September.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
